author: @FrankCurzio
text:
BREAKING: Insuring Oracle's debt against default just hit the highest cost on record.

It now runs 322 basis points (3.22% of the debt every year), after jumping another 22.

It hit the same day Elice crashed on its Korean debut and dragged US futures lower.

The reason is money. Oracle $ORCL borrows to build data centers for its backlog. So its own borrowing gets more expensive at the exact moment it needs to borrow MORE.

That's the mix I worry about with AI builders: heavy debt plus a fear story. It gives short sellers an opening to force more selling, like we saw at SVB.

Back in September I said Oracle's stock moves with the cost of insuring its debt. That cost is now at a record.

I still like the backlog. But I'm not adding until that cost stops rising, because right now Oracle's stock is chained to a number going the wrong way.

author: @FrankCurzio
text:
BREAKING: Korean AI data center stock Elice crashed as much as 32% on its first day of trading.

Elice rents out AI computing power. Its IPO priced at the top of its range. Retail investors asked for more than 400 times the shares on offer.

Then they got crushed.

The model is simple: raise money, buy chips, rent them out. It only works when money is cheap. And as I said Monday, AI borrowing costs just hit their 2026 high.

That's why Nebius ( $NBIS ) at $170.24 gets dragged into headlines like this. It runs the same model in the US. Rising debt costs already squeeze it.

My take: these companies are NOT all the same. I want contracts signed by cash-rich tech giants, or power the company owns outright.

The rest eat every rate hike.

text:
I agree with @michaeljburry and continue to maintain my short exposure to the neocloud trade, particularly $CRWV and $IREN.

The bad news for neoclouds continues. South Korea’s Elice just went public after raising $151M at roughly a $750M valuation. Retail demand was insane: the IPO was oversubscribed more than 400×.

Its business? Renting GPUs and providing the infrastructure to run them.

The stock promptly fell nearly 30% on its first day of trading.

The market is increasingly questioning the economics behind massive GPU capex, debt-funded expansion, and how much durable return these companies can actually generate.
